> I'm struggling to set up the project (first time using VR). Is it required to have hardware for the stereoscopic view? I'd appreciate any help.

This issue only happens with OpenXR  (e.g. it does not occur with the [NativeMobileXR](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_mobilevrinterface.html) interface which is also stereoscopic and requires no setup)

See below on ideas to simulate hardware

> 
> Additionally does disabling jitter (Rendering->Occlusion Culling->Jitter Projection) have any affect?

Disabling Jitter doesn't change anything

For OpenXR you need to at least trick your system into thinking it has VR hardware :D


[The Meta XR Simulator](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=znT4R-qSawg) might be the best way?


On linux I have had success using [ALVR](https://github.com/alvr-org/ALVR) and [PhoneVR](https://github.com/PhoneVR-Developers/PhoneVR) to create a fake HMD by connecting my android phone to my pc over WIFI or usb tethering

There is also with SteamVR's [null_driver](https://github.com/username223/SteamVRNoHeadset) but I haven't been able to get that working

Just for some background info. We cull only once per frame. We actually combine the right and left eye frustums into a larger frustum on which we cull. From the looks of the video we're probably dealing with a situation where the combined frustum isn't large enough and things on the edges are being culled. But its hard to tell for sure. It would be good to verify if this issue also happens with normal frustum culling or is exclusive to occlusion culling, seeing there is nothing in this scene that would cause occlusion.

That said, I wonder if occlusion culling would even be viable in XR because it's possible something is occluded in the combined frustum that is visible to one or both eyes, especially as you look around corners where this scenario becomes increasingly more likely. Seeing we use multiview rendering culling per eye isn't a possibility, unless we want to merge the two culling results, which in most scenes will be more costly than what gets saved in rendering, especially on hardware such as the Quest where TBDR already removes most of the overhead of overdraw.

See https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/servers/rendering/renderer_scene_render.cpp#L52 for the code that combines the frustums, it's possible the resulting frustum is only used for frustum culling and that we haven't properly adjusted occlusion culling to use the same data. 

*edit* just had a closer look, as far as I can tell the combined frustum is used for occlusion culling. So the thing to find out is whether the combined frustum isn't encompassing enough, which is possible because combining two asymmetrical frustums can have some weird edge cases.

> This issue only happens with OpenXR (e.g. it does not occur with the [NativeMobileXR](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_mobilevrinterface.html) interface which is also stereoscopic and requires no setup)

One more thing on this, this points even more to an issue with the combined frustum not being correct.
The mobile VR interface default settings are that for a GearVR using a standard Samsung Note (4 I think).

Quest has different optics and panel sizes so this leads to differently shaped frustums.

You can probably play around with the settings for the mobile VR interface so it creates frustums suitable for Quest and it's likely the issue would appear even with the mobile VR interface. Would be good to experiment with because if this is reproducible, it's much easier to debug then on Quest itself.

> it's much easier to debug then on Quest itself.

It does reproduce on SteamVR when you use QuestLink (or ALVR).. which means you can attach a cpp debugger on your pc!

It seems like OpenXR does something weird with it's projection as it's not centered on the camera origin. (like, maybe the camera origin is the 'neck' rotation position so the camera will rotate around the neck instead of the center of your head?)

> OpenXR
> CAM_PROJ [X: (0.726552, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), Y: (0.0, 0.835475, 0.0, 0.0), Z: (0.000007, -0.193193, -1.000012, -1.0), W: (0.0, 0.0, -0.046693, 0.0)]

The camera is Y-sheared (`Z.y != 0`). It means the viewport is shifted down along the Y axis. I think both eyes are shifted down which explains why the combined matrix is shifted too.

Under such circumstances `Projection::get_viewport_half_extents()` will return garbage on the Y axis. It's clearly visible on the screenshots where all occluders are rendered with a vertical shift.

I just commented on the attached PR. I believe there's a cleaner solution than the one currently implemented.

I've tried both projects in the MRP on a Meta Quest 3 and can reproduce the issue.

> It seems like OpenXR does something weird with it's projection as it's not centered on the camera origin. (like, maybe the camera origin is the 'neck' rotation position so the camera will rotate around the neck instead of the center of your head?)

It's an optimization based around the lense distortion:

https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/unity/unity-asymmetric-fov-faq

It's not _required_ that OpenXR runtimes do this, but they _may_, and we have to be able to deal with it :-)

What Meta calls *asymmetric fov* in the above linked documentation is exactly the definition of Godot's `FRUSTUM` `Camera3D` mode.

This issue should be reproducible with any non-XR `Camera3D` in `FRUSTUM` mode with an offset != 0 (not at my desk right now so I cannot test it).
